messages.author: f2b64d27814968e8
messages.subject: Re: Survey design/stratification
parts:
Hello

I think the main reason for this is that there is no objective way to
define the post-strata. If, for example, you have a block which has a
density gradient from one side to the other, there is a strong temptation
to post-stratify into high and low density blocks. However, there is no
objective way to place the division, and wherever you place it is going to
influence your abundance and variance estimates. This is where the new
spatial analysis techniques will be useful.

Nevertheless I think there might be extreme cases where such
post-stratification is desirable. I have been working on a dataset where
one block has sightings in the north third, and none in the south two
thirds. Here it is easy to post-stratify such that the north sub-block
includes all transects with sightings, and the south sub-block includes all
transects without sightings. When I do the analysis, the abundance estimate
for the north sub-block is virtually the same as that for the original
block (density is much higher of course), but the CV is quite a bit lower
because all of those transects with 0 sightings are gone. This should hold
true as long as the coverage probability is even throughout the block.

Of course such a thing should never happen in a properly designed survey,
where geographical blocks should be related to expected density. However,
this particular survey was designed for another species.

So, is this kind of post-stratification acceptable?

Regards,

Daniel Pike.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Survey design/stratification
parts:
The responses so far miss the real danger of post-stratification. When
you use your data to stratify, you artificially reduce the within-stratum
variance. Consider an extreme case of plot sampling, where you count
number of plants say per plot. You record 0 plants in 80 plots, 1 plant
in 50, and 2 plants in 20. So you define 3 strata, one comprising all
plots with 0 plants, one all plots with 1 plant, and one all plots with 2
plants. You carry out a stratified analysis, and you discover that your
variance is zero - you have apparently determined the exact size of your
population! In Daniel's case, the low-density stratum will yield an
estimate of zero with zero variance. Fine if there really were no animals
there, but it may well be that there were animals present, albeit at a low
density. Similarly, the high-density stratum will yield an underestimate
of variance. Estimation of abundance still tends to be OK - you end up
with an estimate biased high from the high-density stratum, and one biased
low from the low-density stratum, and overall, you get an estimate very
close to the estimate from the unstratified analysis - possibly identical
if you pool across strata for estimating the detection function. If the
strata are coherent geographic blocks, the bias tends to be smaller than
if they comprise high-density bits from throughout the survey region, but
underestimation of variance can still be substantial. A simulation study
could give you an idea of the bias you can expect for your own study.

Steve Buckland
